Indian Standard

FIELDACCEPTANCETESTSTODETERMINETHE HYDRAULICPERFORMANCEOFHYDRAULIC TURBINESJTORAGEPUMPSANDPUMP-TURBINES
NATIONAL FOREWORD This Indian Standard, which is identical with IEC Pub 41(1991) `Field acceptance tests to determine the hydraulic performance of hydraulic turbines, storage~pumps and pump-turbines', issued by the International Electrotechnical Commission (IEC) was adopted by the Bureau of Indian Standards on the recommendation of Rotating Machinery Sectional Committee (ETD 15) and approval of the Electrotechnical Division Council. In the adopted standard certain terminology and conventions are not identical withthose used in Indian Standards, attention is specially drawn to the following: a) b) Wherever the words `International Standard' appear, referring to this standard, they should be read as `Indian Standard'. Comma (,>has been used as a decimal marker while in Indian Standard, the current practice is to use a point (.) as the decimal marker.

Only the English language text in the International Standard has been retained while adopting it in this Indian Standard.

SECTION ONE - GENERAL RULES

Scope and object 1 Scope

1.1 This International Standard covers the arrangements for tests at the site to determine the extent to which the main contract guarantees (see 3.2)~havcbeen satislied. It contains the rules governing their conduct and prcscribcs measures to be taken if any phase of the tests is disputed. It deals with methods of computation of the results as well as the extent, content and style of the final report.

1.2 Model tests, when used for acccptancc purposes, are dealt with in IEC 193 with Amendment No. 1, first supplement 193 A, and in IEC 497. 1.3 Tests of~spccd governing systems arc dealt with in IEC 308. 2 Object The purpose of this standard for licld acceptance tests of hydraulic turbines, storage pumps or pumpturbines, also called the machine, is: to define the terms and quantities which arc used; to specify methods of testing and ways of measuring the quantities involved in order to ascertain ~hc hydraulic pcrformancc of the machine; to dctcrmine if the contract guarantees which fall within the scope of this standard have
bt3X

fulfilled.

The decision to perform field acceptance tests including the definition of their scope is the subject of an agrccmcnt between the purchaser and the supplier of the machine. For this, it has to be examined in each cast, whether the measuring conditions recommended in this standard can be.realized. The influence on ~Ihemeasuring uncertainties, due to hydraulic and civil conditions has to be taken into account. If the actual conditions for field acceptance tests do not allow compliance with the guarantees to be proved, it is recommended that acceptance tests be performed on models (see 1.1.2). 3 Types of ttlnchines In gcncral, Lhis stand`ard applies to any size and type of impulse or reaction turbine, storage pump or pump-turbine. In particular, it applies to machines coupled to electric generators, motors or motorgcncralors. For dc purpose of this standard the term turbine includes a pump-turbine functioning as a turbine and the Lcrmpump includes a pump-turbine functioning as a pump. The term gcncrator includes a motor-gcncrator functioning as a gcncrator and the term motor includes a motor-gcncrator functioning as a motor.

IEC and IS0 Standards rcfcrrcd to in this standard are listed in the prcfacc. If a contradiction is found bclwccn this standard and another IEC or IS0 standard, this standard shall prevail.

1.5 Excluded topics 1.5.1 This standard excludes all matters of a purely commercial interest except those inextricably bound up with the conduct of the tests. 1.5.2 This standard is concerned ncithcr with the structural details of the machines nor with the mechanical properties of their components. 2. Terms, definitions, symbols and units 2.1 Generul The common terms, definitions, symbols and units used throughout the standard arc listed in this clause. Spccialiscd terms arc cxplaincd whcrc they appear. The following terms arc given in 5.1.2 and Figure 11:

1) A run comprises the readings and/or recordings suflicicnt to calculate thc_pcrformancc of the machine
at one operating condition.

2) A point is cstablishcd by one or more conscculivc runs at the same opcraling conditions and unchanged
settings. 3) A test comprises a collection of data and results adcquatc to establish the pcrformancc of the machine over the spccilicd range of operating conditions. The claritication of any conlcslcd term, definition or unit of measure shall bc agreed to in writing by the contracting partics, in advance of the test. 2.2 Units The Tntcrnational System of Units (SI) has been used throughout this standard*. All terms arc given in SI base units or dcrivcd cohcrcnt units (c.g. N instead of kg .. m . s-"). The basic cqualions arc valid using thcsc units. This has to bc taken into account, if other than coherent SI Units arc used for certain data (c.g. kilowatt or megawatt instead of watt for power, kilopascal or bar (= lo5 Pa) instead of Pascal for prcssurc, min-' instead of s-l for rotational speed, etc.). Tcmpcraturcs may bc given in dcgrccs Celsius bccausc thermodynamic (absolute) temperatures (in kelvins) are rarely rcquircd. Any other system of units may bc used but only if agreed to in writing by the contracting parties.

2.3.6 SpeciJic energy terms

In the International System of Units the mass (kg) is one of the base quantities. The cncrgy per unit mass, known as specific cncrgy, is used in this standard asa primary term instead of the cncrgy per local unit weight which is called head and was cxclusivcly used in the former IEC 41 and 198. The latter term (head) has the disadvantage that the weight depends on the accclcration due to gravity 9, which changes mainly with latitude but also with altitude. Nevertheless, the term head will still remain in USC because it is very common. Therefore both related energy terms arc listed, the specific cncrgy terms in this sub-clause and the head terms in 2.3.7. They differ only by the factor 9, which is the local value of acceleration due to gravity. The symbol for specific energy at any section of flow is the small letter e; the symbol for the diffcrcncc of specific energies between any two sections is the capital letter E. The same applies to h and E-I.

Nature and extent of hydraulic performance guarantees 3.1 General 3.1.1 A contract for a regulated or non-regulated* machine should contain guarantees covering at least power, discharge, efficiency (see 3.2.5), maximum momentary overspeed and maximum/minimum momentary pressure, maximum steady state runaway speed (reverse runaway speed in case of a pump). In the case of a pump the guarantees may also cover the maximum zero-discharge specilic hydraulic energy (head) and the zero-discharge power, the latter one with impeller rotating in water and/or in air, for the specified speed. These guarantees are considered as main hydraulic guarantees (see 3.2) and fall within the scope of this standard. Other guarantees (see 3.3) are not covered by this standard. 3.1.2 The purchaser shall arrange ~forthe supplier of the machine to be provided with true, ~fulland acceptable data covering all basins, inlet and outlet structures, waterways between fkpoints of intake and discharge and all parts and equipment relating thereto, all the driven or driving machinery whether electric or not and the revolving parts thereof, and all govcmors, valves, gates and allied mechanisms.

3.1.3 The purchaser shall bc rcsponsiblc Xor specifying the values of all the parameters on which guarantees arc based. including water quality and temperature", specik hydraulic cncrgics of the plant (see 2.3.6.4) and spccilic hydraulic energy losses (see 2.3.6.6), for the study of the plant, particularly the correct inlet and outlet conditions of the machine and for the co-ordination of what concerns the interaction between the machine and the waterways. Should the operational and guaranteed ranges differ, hc shall indicate the limits of the operation.

3.1.4 If the clcctric gcncrator or motor is to bc used for measuring turbine or pump power (see 2.3.8.3), such clcctric gcncralor or motor and its auxiliaries shall be given appropriate tests. It should be a condition of the contract that the supplier of the hydraulic unit or his representative shall have the right to be present at such tests. A ccrtilied copy of the generator or motor test calculations and results shall be given to the supplier of the hydraulic machine. 3.2 Main guarantees 3.2.1 Praclical plant operation Practical plant operation usually involves some variation in specific hydraulic energy (head). Therefore specifications shall state the specific hydraulic energies to which guarantees shall apply. For practical reasons a transient test may not be conducted at the same time as a steady-slate performance -test.

* A rcgulatcd machine is a machine in which the flow is controlled by a flow-controlling device such as guide vanes. needle(s), and/or runncr/impclier blades. A single regulated machine is a regulated machine with one flow-controlling dcvicc; a double regulated machine is a rcgulaled machine with two flow-controlling devices. A non-regulated machine is a machine in which no flow-controlling device is provided. ** If the water temperature during the acceptance test is significantly the relevant scale effect should be taken into account. different from the specified value (e.g. more than 10�C).

3.2.2 Power

Power guarantees may bc rcquircd at one or more specified speeds for: a regulated turbine: power to be reached at one or more specilied specific hydraulic cncrgics (see Figure 10 a); a non-regulated turbine: power to be reached and power not to be exceeded over a specified specific hydraulic energy range* (see Figure 10 b); a non-regulated/regulated pump: power not to be exceeded over a specified specific hydraulic energy range (see Figure 10 c).
3.2.3 Discharge

Discharge guarantees may be required at one or more specified speeds for:

4 a regulated turbine: discharge to bc reached at one or more specified specific hydraulic energies (see
Figure 10 a);

b) a non-rcgulatcd turbine: discharge to bc reached over a specilicd specilic energy range (this guarantee
is usually rcplaccd by the corresponding power guarantee, see 3.2.2 6) and discharge not to be exceeded (set Figure 10 b);

Cl a non-rcgulaled/rcgulatcd pump: discharge over a specified specific hydraulic energy range, including
values to bc reached or not to be exceeded** (see Figure 10 c). The guaranteed discharge may be referred to the ambient pressure (see 2.3.4.5). ~3.2.4 EJ"ciency 3.2.4.1 Regulated turbine efficiency guarantees may be required at one or more specilied speeds and specific hydraulic cncrgies: n) at one or more individual spccilkd powers or discharges or as a curve (see Figure 10 a);
b) as wcightcd avcragc cfficicncies*** over a range of power~or discharge;

c) as arithmetic avcragc cfticicncics*** over a range of power or discharge. 3.2.4.2 Non-regulated turbine or non-regulated/regulated pump efficiency guarantees may be required at one or more specified speeds: a) at one or more individual spccikd specific hydraulic energies or as a curve (see Figures 10 b and 10 c);
6) as weighted average efficiencies*** over a specified range of specific hydraulic energies;

c) as arithmetic avcragc efficiencies*** over a specified range of specific hydraulic energies.

3.2.5 Choice of power, discharge and efficiency guarantees It is recommended that the contraclual agrccmcnts avoid fixing more than one guarantee for correlated quLantilies; for instance, in the case of a regulated turbine efficiency shall be guaranteed versus discharge or power, but not versus discharge and power.

4. Organisation

of test

4.1 Adequate provision for test

It is recommended that attention should be given to provisions for testing when the plant is being designed. This applies particularly to the arrangements for measuring discharge and specilic hydraulic energy. It is suggested that during the design stage of the plant and the machines to be tested, provision is made for more than one method of measuring discharge and pressure (or free water level). The methods of measurement should be fully covered in the specifications and in the contracts. The conditions should also be considered when a prospective purchaser, or the engineers, submit an enquiry to possible suppliers. It should be stated at this time that the acceptance tests shall be performed in accordance with all applicable requirements of this standard. Any anticipated deviation from this standard should bc clearly stated. 4.2 Authority for test Subject to the provisions of the contract, both parties shall have equal rights in determining the test methods and procedures and in selecting all test personnel. The test may be entrusted to experts who hold independent positions with respect to both parties. If so, they and the Chief of test together with the contracting partics shall have tinal authority in selecting all other test personnel.

4.3 Personnel The selection ofpcrsonncl to conduct the test and procedures in connection thcrcwith arc matters of prime importance. 4.3.1 Chief of test A Chief of test shall be appointed by agreement between the two parties. Hc should be compctcnt to supcrvisc all of the calibrations, mcasurcmcnts and calculations necessary to determine the performance _ of the machine. Hc shall cxcrcise authority over all observers. He shall supervise the conduct of the test in accordance with this standard and any written agrccmcnt made prior to the test by the contracting pat-tics. He shall bc rcsponsiblc for the calibration of all test instruments and for all test mcasurcmcnts. He shall report on test conditions and bc responsible for the computation of results including the determination of the mcasurcment uncertainties and the preparation of the final report. On any question pertaining to the test his decision, subject to the provisions of 4.5.1,4.7.6 and 4.9.1, shall be final. 4.3.2 Choice of personnel The testing team shall have the ncccssary competence and experience for the correct installation and utilization of the measuring equipment. 4.3~3 Presence at test Both purchaser and supplier of the machine shall be entitled to have rcprcscntativcs prcscnt at all tests in order to verify that they are performed in accordance with this standard and any prior written agrcemcnts. 4.4 Preparation for test 4.4.1 Submission of drawings and relevant data All drawings of importance for the test and all relevant data, documents, spccidcations, certilicatcs and reports on operating conditions shall be placed at thedisposal of the Chief of test.

30

IS/rEC 41(1991)

4.4.2 Inspection on site Shortly before the start of the test, the unit and all test cquipmcnt shall bc subjcctcd to thorough inspection by rcprcsentatives of both partics and the Chief of test to cnsurc that conditions arc such that the performance of the machine may be judged equitably (see also 4.8). It shall bc veriticd that:

4 all machinery is complete and according to specifications;
b) the scales indicating the opening of the guide vanes and/or runner/impeller blades, where applicable, or
the opening of nozzles and deflectors are calibrated and the relationship between openings is correct. The scales shall have sufiicient resolution and will be accessible throughout the test. Provisions shall exist to block effectively the guide vane or nozzle openings during each point to promote stability and accurate repetition of openings;

Cl no water passages are obstructed or restricted by any foreign matter;
d) no wear has taken place on vital parts, particularly in the form of cavitation damage to runners/impellers, guide vanes, nozzles or other water passage components and/or damage to wearing rings or labyrinths, that could have a significant effect on efficiency; e) all pressure taps, piczomctric tubes and connecting pipes have been properly formed and located and are clear of obstruction. 4.4.3 Measurements before test The dimensions of the conduit at and between measurement sections, when required, shall bc mcasurcd accurately before the unit is opcratcd. A main bench mark for levels shall bc established. All secondary bench m`arks (levelling rcfercncc points) in the specific hydraulic energy measuring system shall be refcrrcd lo it. All bench marks shall bc retained undisturbed until the final report has been accepted. When the indirect method of powcr~measurement is used, the results of the gencrator/molor efficiency test should prcfcrably bc available prior to the hydraulic machine pcrformancc test. In case such information is missing the gmarantccd values of generator/motor for losses may be used for preliminary computation of the results. 4.5 Agreement on test procedure 4.5.1 Approval of procedure The test programmc and proccdurc shall be prepared by the Chief of test, taking into consideration the plans previously prcparcd according to 4.1. All arrangements and plans shall bc submitted to both purchaser and supplier in ample time for considcralion and agreement. Approval or objection shall bc given in writing.

4.5.2 Date of test The acccptancc test shall not take place until the commissioning tcsls, including speed and prcssurc variation trials, have been conducted. See also IEC 545 and 805. It is for the purchaser to dccidc, with rcspcct to plant operation and flow conditions, on the dam of the acccptancc test. This shall bc within the contract guarantee period and prcfcrably within six months after the machine has been handed over to the purchaser, unless otherwise agreed by both p`arlicsin writing.

WIEC

41( 1991)

4.5.3 General programme

The general programme shall be drafted by the Chief of test and shall include particulars concerning the following items: 4.5.3.1 Spccilic hydraulic cncrgy for acccptancc test In those cases where guarantees are given for more than one specific hydraulic energy the general programme shall state at which value or values of specilic hydraulic cncrgy the acceptance test shall be carried out, on the basis of the purchaser's instructions.
4.5.3.2 Machines to be tested for efliciency

The contract shall specify whether scvcral or only one of a group-of identical machines arc to be tested with regard to efficiency. The general programme shall specify the actual machine or machines to bc tested. If only one is to be tcstcd, it is recommcndcd~that the machine shall bc chosen by mutual agreement between purchaser and supplier. 4.5.3.3 Extent and duration of test The general programmc shall include a statement on the number of points to be taken and the corresponding operating conditions. The number of points to be obtained dcpcnds on the nature and extent of the guanntccs and shall bc dccidcd by the Chief of test. Prescriptions on the number of points, the mode of machine operation and other rclatcd items which shall be included in the gcncral programmc are d&tiled in 5.1 for the steady state pcrformancc test and in 7.1 for the transient operation test. 4.6 Instrumenrs 4.6.1 Identijicafion of instruments The maker, serial number or other identilication, and owner of each instrument shall be stated in the linal report. 4.6.2 Calibralion of inslruments All instruments, including electrical instrument transformers, shall bc calibrated before the test and both purchaser and supplier may witness their calibration. Whether calibrated on or off site, the validity~of all calibrations shall be vcrilied by the Chief of~tcst. In the case of an off-site calibration, a valid ccrtillcalc, acccptablc to both the purchaser and the supplier, shall be provided. All ncccssary correction and pre-test calibration CU~~CS of the instruments to bc employed shall be available before any test is carried out. Unless omitted by agreement, all calibrations shall be repeated after completion of the test. The dates and places of all calibrations shall be stated in the final report. The institutions that have performed the calibrations shall state in writing whether the variations between pre- and post-test calibrations are within acceptable limits. If such is the case, their arithmetical means shall be used in thecomputation of the final results. If not, tither a special agreement shall be made as to how any disputed values shall be used or the test shall bc repeated. 4.7 Observalions 4.7.1 Observalion sheets Observation sheets which clearly indicate the items to be measured shall be prepared for use at each of the various stations. A suflicient number of copies of the observation sheets shall bc prepared and each party to the test shall immediately be handed a complete set. These observation sheets shall:

32

IS/lEC 41( 1991)

a) record the power plant designation and the serial number of each machine to be tested and the serial
numbers of the instruments as well as any other essential information to identify all instruments and their location;

b) record the positions of all nozzles needles, runner/impeller blades, and/or adjustable guide vanes; C>record all rcadings made at each observation station and the time at which each reading was taken,
togcthcr with any circumstances dcscrving attention;

4 bc signed by the particular obscrvcr; Cl provide for other necessary signatures (see 4.7.5);

n

bc examined by, and copies given to, all parties before the end of the test.

4.7.2 Instrument reudings

All readings of direct-reading instruments shall be taken during the same period of time and the frequency of the reading shall be decided by the Chief of test. Care shall be taken that the time interval between rcadings does not coincide with the period, or any multiple thereof, of any steady state oscillations in the instrumentation or machine under test. Visual averaging is to be avoided, if possible, bccausc this inevitably introduces some personal bias (see also 5.2.1). All readings for the preliminary test (5.1.3) shall bc taken with the same care and accuracy as for the acceptance test.

4.7.3 lnstrumen t recordings

Instrument recordings (analog or digital) may be used provided that the accuracy and resolution of 1.11~ records are comparable to or bcttcr than instantaneous readings of direct reading test instruments. All recordings shall be avcragcd or intcrprctcd under the direct supervision of the Chief of test, using the most suitable and accurate techniques.
417.4Preliminary calculation

After completion of the test, the readings and recordings shall be cxamincd by both panics and rcprcscntative results shall be provisionally computed on site using the prc-test calibrations. All errors or inconsistcncics thereby discovered shall be eliminated or taken into account. Only on this basis may the test be tcrminatcd and the test instruments rcmovcd (see 4.6.2).

4.7.5 Signing of readings and recordings

The test recordings shall bc signed by the Chief of test and by reprcscntativcs of both parties. 4.7.6 Procedure in case of dispute or repetition If thcrc is any dissatisfaction with the test for clearly explained masons stated in writing, the dissatisIicd party shall have the right to demand additional tests. Agreement at this stage shall not preclude either party from cxprcssing dissatisfaction with the test when the final results arc available. In such cast, either party and/or the Chief of test may demand a rcpcat test. If final agreement as to the conduct of such a test cannot bc rcachcd, the matter shall bc rcfcrrcd to an independent arbitrator acceptable to all panics. The contract should fix the responsibility for the cost of any repcat test. 4% Inspcclion after test If rcqucstcd by cithcr party or the Chief of test, the unit and all test equipment shall bc available for inspection within two days after completion of-the test. 5. Test conditions and procedure 5.1 General lest procedure 5.1 .l Mehods of measurement The methods to be used for the measurement or computation of discharge, power, specific hydraulic energy, efficiency, speed and losses shall be stated in the general programme. They arc described in Clauses 9 to 14. An additionalindex discharge measurement is recommended to overcome any difficulties that may arise from the chosen method. The index test methods are describedin Clause 15.

5.1.2 Number of points, runs and readings A performance curve such as that illustrated by Figure 10 a requires a minimum of six and prcfcrably tight or ten points. Each point will be obtained from one or more runs (see 2.1 and 5.1.3). The number of measurements taken during a run depends upon the methods of measurement used, but for a statistical lrcatmcnt (see Appendix C and D) at least five readings of direct-reading instruments per run arc to bc taken over an agreed time or over the duration of any time-based measurements. Figure 11 shows an cxamplc of a test schedule. The interval of time during which all instantaneous readings and instrument recordings are made for each run shall gcncrally bc the same for each point. For some types of measurcmcnt such as the transit time method of discharge measurement, the time necessary to complete a run may vary significantly with discharge. It may then be appropriate to adjust the time interval between instantaneous rcadings so that each run contains the same number of readings or at least an agreed minimum number of readings. The sole exception is for any pressure-time method diagrams which shall be started within approximately 15 s after the last instantaneous reading or~theend of recording of the other quantities.

51.3 Recommended lest procedwes

Two proccdurcs are recommended. The first (Method A) consists oftesting a number of points over a range of operating conditions and drawing performance curves through them. The second (Method I3) is based on testing several times one or a few specified operating points: Both methods may bc supplemented as necessary by index tests. For Method A, the quality of the measurements is judged by the deviations of the points from the best smooth mean curve drawn through them. For Method B, not applicable when test conditions can be maintained constant for a short time only, the quality of the measurements is judged by the deviations of the results of the individual runs from their arithmetical mean value at the operating point considered. If a guarantee is given for peak cfliciency, @t the corresponding operating conditions arc unknown or unspecified, a preliminary index test shaI1be carried out to determine these operating conditions, after which the necessary complete runs shall be made (see also 51.4). A preliminary test should be carried out to instruct all participants in their respective duties and to verify satisfactory operation of all test equipment or to correct or improve it, if necessary. During both the preliminary and acceptance tests, all possible cross-checks of data and results should be carried out to rcducc or eliminate errors. Provisional results should be calculated and plotted as fast as the data are gathered. These running plots of discharge and power versus gate opening for turbines or discharge and power versus specilic hydraulic energy for pumps may reveal testing errors or abnormalities in the operating characteristics of the machine which require further investigation. It may not be practicable to include all of the instrument corrections in the provisional results.

5.1.3.1 Method A This method shall bc used when performance curves over a range of operating conditions must be obtained (see also Appendix D) or when the test conditions can be maintained constant (see 5.2.1) only for a short~timc. The test programme shall deline: a) the range of operating conditions to be covered by the test; b) the number and scqucncc of operating points to be tested; c) the guide vanc/ncedlc, runncr/impcllcr blade and speed settings; cl) any supplcmcntary index test to bc made. 5.1.3.2 Method B This mcthod may bc used only if the operating conditions can be maintained constant (52.1) over the whole test time necessary to establish the machine performance at the opcraling point spccilicd (SW also Appendix C). The test programmc shall dcline the minimum number of runs, but in no case shall the number bc less than five at the same operating conditions. If tests at more than one operating condition arc required, each of them shall have the same number of runs.

3s

ISIIEC 41( 1991)

The test programme shall also deline: a) the number and sequence of operating points to be tested; 6) the guide vane/needle, runner/impeller blade and speed settings: c) any supplementary index test to bc made. 5.1.4 Particular procedurefor double regulated turbines Eflicicncy and power tests shall be made with the optimum relationship between guide vane and runner blade openings. The optimum relationship can be established either during acccptancc test or by previous index test. In this case, the optimum relationship must be established under the same hydraulic conditions as for the acceptance test, using for each of at least five blade openings, at least live difercnt guide vane openings.

5.1.5 Particular procedure for single regulated or double regulated pumps If possible, tests of these machines shall be carried out over the specified range of specific hydraulic energy and discharge. Efficiency and power tests shall be made with the openings of guide vanes and/or runner/impeller blades adequate to check the contract guarantees. These openings must be established under the same hydraulic conditions as for the acceptance test. In the case of a double regulated pump the relationship between guide vane and impeller blade openings can be established during the acceptance test or by aprevious index test. When adequate changes in water levels are not possible, discharge throttling and/or speed variation, if possible, may be used to obtain the necessary range of specific hydraulic energy.

ISAEC 41(1991) 6.2 Uncertainties in measurements* and presentation of results 62.1 Definition of error The error in the measurement of a quantity is the difference between that mcasurcmcnt and the true value of the quantity. No measurement of a physical quantity is free from uncertainties arising from systematic errors and random errors. Systematic errors cannot be reduced by repeating measurement since they arise from the characteristics of the measuring apparatus, the installation, and the operation conditions. Howcvcr, a reduction in the random error may be achieved by repetition of measurements since the random error of the mean of n independent measurements is fi times smaller than the random e.rror of an individual measurement (see Appendix C). 6.2.2 Definition of uncertainty The range within which the true value of a measured quantity can be expected to lit with a suitably high probability is termed the "uncertainty of themeasurement". For the purposes of this standard, the probability to-be used shall be 95 % level. 6.2.3 Types -

of errors

There are three types of error which must be considered: spurious errors; random errors; systematic errors.

6.2.3.1 Spurious errors Thcsc are errors such as human errors, or instrument malfunction, which invalidate a measurement: for cxamplc, the transposing of numbers in recording data or the prescncc of pockets of air in leads from a water lint to a manometer. Such errors should not be incorporated into any statistical analysis and the measurement must bc discarded. Where the error is not large enough to make the result obviously invalid, some rcjcction criteria should bc applied to decide whether the data point should bc rejected or retained. Unless otherwise agreed, the Grubbs test described in Appendix B is recommended for testing possible outhers; other tests, such as the Dixon test given in IS0 5168, may be used by agreement. It is ncccssary to rccalculatc the standard deviation of the distribution of results after applying the outlier test if any data points arc discarded. It should also be emphasized that outlier tests may be applied only if thcrc is an indcpendcnt technical reason for believing that spurious errors may exist: data should not bc thrown away lightly. 6.2.3.2 Random errors Random errors arc caused by numerous, small, independent influences which prevent a measurcmcnt system from dclivcring the same reading when supplied with the same-input value of the quantity being mcasurcd. The mcasurcmcnts dcvialc from the mean in accordance with the laws of chance, such that the distribution usually approaches a normal distribution as the number of mcasurcmcnts is incrcascd. The random error is influenced by the care taken during measurements, the number of mcasurcmcnts and the operating conditions. The scaltcr of readings observed during a point results from the combination of the random error arising from the instrumentation and of the influcncc of the opcnling conditions.
l

See IS0 5168.

44

I!yIEc 41(1991)

6.2.3.3 Estimation of the uncertainty associated with random error Statistical methods for estimating the uncertainty associated with random error are discussed in Appendices C and D. When the sample size is small, it is necessary to correct the statistical results that are based on a normal distribution by means of Student's t values, as explained in these appendices. Student's t is a factor which compensates for the uncertainty in the standard deviation increasing as the sample size is reduced. The uncertainty corresponding to a lcvcl of 95 % is written (fr)aa. An agreement prior to the test shall specify the maximum permissible value &:f, of~the uncertainty bandwidth due to random errors. If more than 5 %~ofthe results are outside this range, an accurate analysis will be made and the measurements will be repeated or a new value of the uncertainty bandwidth due to random errors will be agreed. 6.2.3.4 Systematic errors Systematic errors are those which cannot bc reduced by increasing the number of measurements if the equipment and conditions of measurements remain unchanged. The systematic error of a measurement depends partly on the residual error in the instrument or measuring system at the start of the test. At that time, all removable errors will have been eliminated by calibration, careful measurement of dimensions, proper installation, etc. The error still remaining is called systematic error (bias) and always exists, however small. The systematic error is largely controlled by the choice of measuring method, and the operating conditions; for example, the value of the kinetic energy calculated w-iththe mean velocity can differ from its true value if the velocity distribution at the measuring section is not suflicicntly regular. Systemadc errors do not affect the repeatability of measurements during a test. Prior to any test, an agreement should be reached on an expected band of systematic uncertainty within the range given in the first column of Table AI, Appendix A. It must be emphasised that the values for systematic uncertainties listed in the second column are expected uncertainties when the mcasuremcnts arc made in normal conditions by experiencedpersonnel with an apparatus of high quality, in accordance with the provisions of the standard. The actual value of systematic uncertainty usually depends on many factors, some of which can only be evaluated after the test. A review of these factors shall be made and an agreement bctwccn the parties concerned established whether the expected uncertainties have to be changed on technical grounds or not.

6.2.3.5 Estimation of the uncertainty associated with systematic errors The uncertainty associated with systematic errors cannot be assessed experimentally without changing the equipment or conditions of measurcmcnt. This change can indicate an order of magnitude of the systcmalic error and should be applied whcnevcr possible. The alternative is to make a subjective judgcment on the basis of experience and consideration of the equipment involved. The first step in the estimation of this uncertainty is to identify those aspects of the measurement that can affect its value; the second step is to allocate uncertainty limits to allow for each of these effects. This may bc done, in part at least, by statistical analysis*.

* See for example IS0 5168.

45

IS/IEC 41( 1991)

If the error has a unique known value then this shall be added to (or subtracted from) the result of the measurement and the uncertainty in the measurement due to this source is then taken as zero. If the systematic error of a measuring device is unknown but its error limits (class of accuracy) are specitied, the interval between them may bc assumed as the systematic uncertainty of that device with aconfidence~level better than 95 %. Systematic errors usually are considerably larger than random errors for the highest quality field test. Actually, notwithstanding the difference exposed above between systematic and random uncertainties, the probability distribution of the possible values of each systematic component is essentially gaussian and the systematic uncertainty f, is computed from the individual systematic' uncertainties by the rootsum-squares method; for example, the systematic uncertainty of efficiency (fV), is computed from the individual systematic uncertainties in discharge (fo),, specific hydraulic energy.(f,), and power (f,,), by:

See also Clause A2 of Appendix A.
6.2.4 Total uncertainty

The total uncertainty in a measurement (fJ is obtained by combining the systematic (f.) and random (fr) uncertainties (see 6.2.3.3 and 6.2.3.5). It defines a range within which the true value is assumed to have a probability of 95 % to lie, and any point in this~rangeis equally valid. Given the same type of probability distribution of the systematic and random uncertainties (see 6.2.3.5), they can be combined by the root-sum-squares method. The~total uncertainty is thus given by:
f, = f

(fsz + fZ)""

6.2.5 Analysis of resulls

The method of analysis and presentation of results describedhereafter with particular reference to comparison with guarantees is recommended. Appendix A contains estimates of systematic uncertainties; Appendices C and D provide enough information to make simple estimates of random unccrtaintics; Appendix B describes a method for rejecting outliers.

6.2.6 Presentalion of resulls

Taking into account the total uncertainties calculated as explained in 6.2.4, each measured point should be represented on a diagram by an ellipse. The axes of this ellipse represent the total uncertainty, at a conlidcnce lcvcl of 95 %, in the two quantities chosen as coordinates of the diagram. Any point within this cllipsc is equally valid. If a curve is guaranteed (guarantee given within a range of powers, for instance), an uncertainty band corresponding to the upper and lower envelopes of these ellipses is superimposed to the best fitted curve drawn through the test points (see Appendix D). All the points within this band are equally valid and thus this band constitutes an acceptable bandwidth for comparison with guarantees. In some cases, for cxamplc, when the guarantee curve is plotted against specific hydraulic cncrgy, the limits of the total uncertainty bandwidth can bc obtained by reducing the cllipscs to their principal axis.

7. `l&t conditions 7.1 Test condifions

and procedure

7.1.1 General Transient operating conditions (e.g. load rejections, power failure etc.) cause prcssurc and speed variations dependent on the type of machine and on the movement of the shut-off dcviccs (Cc. guide vanes, nccdlcs and/or valves). In addition, superimposed pressure variations and iluctuations of significant magnitude, not directly attributable to operational changes, can occur in some applications (c.g. pumpturbines). In these casts, they should be the subject of a separate guarantee in the contract. The test should bc pcrformcd, if possible, under the specified worst conditions. For each plant the worst conditions should bc determined carefully and agreed upon before the test.

7.1.2. Speed varialions 7.1.2.1 Momentary ovcrspccd The definition is given in 2.3.4.13. For most turbines, maximum momentary overspeed (see 2.3.4.14) will occur following sudden load rcjcction when power is being rcduccd to zero. 7.1.2.2 Steady stale runaway speed Regulated machines are normally protected from full runaway speed condition through an adcquatc closing device. Accordingly for most machines, steady state runaway speed is not normally reached and runaway speed therefore may be considered as an unusual or extraordinary condition. Unless otherwise agreed,it is recommended not to carry out steady state runaway speed tests. If carried out they should be performed at reduced specific hydraulic energy in order to keep the physical stress of the machines - particularly of the electrical machinery - low in comparison with the stress which may occur at tests under the full specific hydraulic energy. For non-regulated machines and for regulated machines with shut-off devices which have long closing times, steady state runaway speed will normally be exceeded during load rejection which is pcrformcd during commissioning. Thcrcforc a separate steady state runaway test is not necessary.

7.1.3 Prcmirc variations The maximum momentary prcssurc on the high pressure side and the minimum momentary prcssurc on the low prcssurc side of a turbine normally occur during Lhc shut-down operation when a spccificd load is rcduccd to zero. The minimum momentary pressure on the high prcssurc side and the maximum momentary pressure on the low prcssurc side normally occur during the opening movement of the shut-off dcvicc beginning from zero or from no-load opening. For pumps, the minimum prcssurc on the high pressure side and the maximum prcssurc on the low pressure side occur during a power failure. Unless othcrwisc spccificd the momentary pressure shall bc measured at the rcfcrcncc sections.

IWIEC 41( 1991)

I.2 `I& procedure and instrumentation 7.2.1 General requirements

Since the pressure and speed varialions depend on the movement of the shut-off devices, all three quantities shall be recorded simultaneously. 7.2.2 Measurement of speed variations Instrumentation for measurcmcnt of speed variations shaIl bc capable of attaining a measurement total uncertainty of fl, 0%. 7.2.3 Measurement of pressure variations Electrical pressure transducers or spring-type indicators may bc used for recording pressure variations. The measuring devices shall be insensitive to mechanical vibration and shall be connected directly (flush) to the pcnstock wall whenever this is possible. If the instrument cannot be directly connected to the pcnstock, the piping shall be as short and straight as possible and made of metal. Flexible tubes are not allowed.

Air shall bc purged out of the piping before measurement. Purchaser and supplier shall agree upon an upper frcqucncy limit up to which pressure fluctuations shall bc accounted for. The measuring chain including transducer and piping shall reproduce fluctuations with frcqucncics lower than the limit without distortion by damping or rcsonancc in the measuring tap. Fluctuations with higher frequency shall be removed by appropriate filtering. The basis of thelimiting frequency for the filter is given by the specitic frequency characteristics of the hydraulic system. The maximum permissible value of measurement total uncertainty shall be flO0 x p-`lz5% (where p is in pascals). 8. SECTION FOUR -

METHODS OF MEASUREMENT

9. Introduction 9.1 Eficiency A field acceptance test on a hydraulic machine in accordance with this standard aims at comparing the achieved hydraulic performance with the guarantees given by the supplier. This involves the evaluation of absolute values of specific hydraulic energy, discharge, mechanical power, rotational speed and efficiency. Efticiency may be calculated from the mechanical power P exchanged with the electrical machine and the hydraulic power Ph cxchangcd with the water. According to the definition given in 2.3.9.3, the efticiency of the hydraulic machine is: for a turbine, 17= PIP,, for a pump. `7= PJP The dctcrmination of the hydraulic power and of the mechanical power is dealt with in 9.2 and 9.3 rcspcctivcly. This method involves the mcasurcment of discharge (see Clause lo), specific hydraulic energy (see Clause 1l), electrical or mechanical power (by direct method) (see Clause 12) and rotational speed (see Clause 13). Efficiency may also bc obtained in a more direct way from the water tcmperaturc increase due to the losses, using the thermodynamic method (SWClause 14). Efficiency is then cxpresscd as:
~=%`r],,,= AP Ef+`E, &Em 17=7lh*7),= Em

for a pump.

The basic advantage of the thermodynamic method is represented by the fact that it dots not require the measurement of the discharge. Bcsidcs these methods, an index test is often conducted on site. In normal conditions, such a test gives only relative information on the discharge and thus on the efticiency. However, when the relative discharge measuring method is calibrated by an absolute method of discharge measurement, the index method may bc further used to extend an acccptancc test to running conditions for which the uncertainty of the absolute mcasurcmcnts becomes too large. In such cases, the index test (set Clause 15) can be considered as a part of the licld acccptancc test. 9.2 Hydruulic power 9.2.1 Definition The detinition of hydraulic power is given in 2.3.8.1. Its evaluation requires knowledge of the specific hydraulic energy of the machine and of the mass flow rate through the high pressure reference section (subscript 1). The formula is:

IS/IEC 41( 1991)

9.2.2 Massjlow rate

The mass flow rate (see 2.3.4.2) at rcfcrcncc section 1 may differ from that at the measuring section, due to the transfer of water to or from the syslcm bctwecn thcsc two sections. All uansfcrs not ncccssary to the proper operation of the unit shall be stopped during the measurements (stilling period included) lo avoid increased uncertainty and multiple measurements of discharge. Account shall be taken of the remaining transfers. 9.2.3 Hydraulic power correction
912.3.1 Analysis of correction

The correction term AP, will bc evaluated after a relevant analysis of contractual d&&ions and local conditions. As a rule, hydraulic power transfer necessary to the proper operation of the hydraulic machine shall bc charged to it. This analysis shall bc conducted taking into account: whether the auxiliary discharge is injected in or taken from the main circuit bcforc or after the discharge measuring section and before or after the machine; whcthcr the auxiliary discharge is used or not for the proper hydraulic machine operation; whcthcr the machine opcralcs as a turbine or as a pump.

For cxamplc, any waler taken off bctwccn the discharge measuring section and a machine in turbine mode and not used for the turbine operation will induce a negative contribution to P,,.
9.2.3.2 Evaluation of correction

The mass flow rate of transferred water and the relevant spcciiic hydraulic cncrgy shall bc used for evaluating each correction. This relevant specitic hydraulic energy may differ from E, cspccially in multistage machines. Since such transfers are generally a small fraction of the main discharge, a simple evaluation will be sufftcicnt and will have no signihcant cffcct on the measuring uncertainty. It is rccommcndcd that all water transfers are spccitied in the contract and may be checked at time of test. Since most bansfers necessary to the correct operation of the machine arc needed for specihc purposes (for instance, cooling of the bearings), and therefore the relevant losses arc measured or easily cvaluatcd, a spccitic mcasurcmcnt for AP,, evaluation will then seldom be necessary. An approximated value of transfer specific hydraulic energy may also be used.
9.2.3.3 Cast of the thermodynamic method

Whcncvcr the thermodynamic method is used, the hydraulic power is notmnecdedfor the cvalualion of the cfficicncy. Howcvcr, if there arc water transfers, it is necessary to take them into account (set 14.5.3).

59

IS/IEC 41(1991) 9.2.4 Water density

The dcnsily of water shall be determined for the pressure and the temperature prevailing in the discharge measuring section. Values of pure water density are tabulated in Appendix E, Table EII. In some cases, it may bc necessary to measure the density of water, for example by a static method (see 11.4.7.1).

9.3 Mechanical power Normally the power (mechanical power of the machine) is determined electrically by measuring the generator output (active output power) or motor input (active input power) and taking into account the mechanical and electrical losses in the electrical machine, and all the other losses specified in 2.3.8.3. This method is called indirect. In the case of small units of low capacity the direct method may be used; it consists of determining the power at the hydraulic machine~shaft by means of devices measuring torque and rotational speed and taking account of the relevant losses (see 2.3.8.3). The direct method has to bc used for hydraulic machines which arc not directly coupled to an electrical machine. Considering the development of torque measuring techniques, it is recommended that the Chief of test makes an analysis of the feasibility and of the expected uncertainty of the direct method. AI1the clcmcnts necessary to determine the mechanical power by the indirect method are given in 12.1: clectricat power measurement (12.1.1) and measurement or calculation of the various losses (12.1.2). The mechanical power measurement by the direct method is dealt with in 12.2. 10. Discharge 10.1 General The measurement of discharge in a hydroelectric or pumped storage plant can bc performed with the desired accuracy only when the spccilic requirements of the chosen method are satishcd. It is therefore in the inlercst of the partics involved to sclcct the method(s) to be used for an acceptance test at an early stage in the design of the plant because later provision may be expensive or even impracticable. It is suggcstcd that provision be made for two methods, for instance one method for gross discharge mcasurcment and another giving information on the flow pattcms.

10.1.1 Choice of the method of measurement 10.1.1.1 The choice of the method(s) for measuring discharge may dictate the conduct and duration of the performance test. Some of the factors that may affect this choice are:
a) limitations imposed by the design of the plant;

b) cost of installation and special equipment; c) limitations imposed by plant operating conditions, for example draining of the system, constant load or discharge operation, etc. 10.1.1.2 The discharge ~measuremcnt for an IEC acceptance test shall bc made by an absolute method. Ncvcrthclcss, it may bc useful to resort to relative methods (index methods) cithcr to gain supplcmcntary information or to make easier some operations (see 151.3).

60

IS/xEC 41(1991) The absolute methods described in this standard (see 10.2to 10.8) arc: the velocity-area method by means of current-meters or Pitot tubes, the pressure-time method (Gibson method), tracer methods either by transit-time or dilution measurement, standardized thin-plate weirs, standardized differential pressure dcviccs, and volumetric gauging. In addition Appendix J~describes the acoustic method which is optional. Moreover, the thermodynamic method of efliciency measurement (see Clause 14) permits discharge to bc obtained as a derived quantity from efficiency, specific energy and power measurements. Relative methods such as the Winter-Kennedy method, non-standardized differential pressure devices, non-standardized weirs or flumes, certain simpleforms of acoustic method or local velocity mcasurcmcnt with a single current-meter may bc used to obtain a relative value of the discharge or even an absolute value if lhcy arc calibrated in situ by comparison with an absolute method. Some of these relative methods arc described in Clause 15. 10.1.1.3 Only the velocity-area method by means of current-meters or Pitot tubes and to some extent the acoustic method using several paths provide information on the flow pattern.

10.1.2 Accuracy of measurement 10.1.2.1 Clause 10 prcscnts all the rcquircmcnts for satisfactory mcasurcmcnts and cslimatcs the syslcmatic uncertainty to be cxpccted when these rcquircments are satisfied. A method of measurement is described in detail only when no standardized proccdurc exists clscwhcrc. Whcnevcr possible, rcferencc has been made to existing standards, especially to those published by the International Organization for Standardization (ISO) which arc particukarly suited to the precise rcquircmcnts of this test standard. In some cases, the prescriptions of IS0 Standards have been supplcmcntcd by a few additional rcquircmcnts which appear necessary for the particular scope of this test standard. 10.1.2.2 The actual values of systematic and random uncertainties shall bc evaluated taking into account the whole measuring system and the operating conditions. The total uncertainty shall bc calculated in accordance with 6.2. 10.1.2.3 Frcqucnlly the accuracy achieved by the chosen method can be estimated only after the results of the , tests at the given plant have been analysed (see 6.2.3.4). The numerical values of systematic uncertainty indicated in this clause arc to be used only as guidance. They are valid only: - with the best conditions of mcasurcment; if all individual rcquircmcnts arc satisfied; and if the testing and analysis arc carried out by qualified and experienced personnel.

If thcsc conditions arc not satisfied, thcrc may be an unpredictable incrcasc in both the systc.malic and random error of the discharge mcasurcmcnt.

61

IS/IEC 41( 1991) 10.1.3 General requirements 10.1.3.1Steadiness of the flow

Whatever the method used, a discharge measurement for acceptance test is valid only if the flow is steady or nearly steady during each run. It may be assumed steady if the variations in generator or motor power, in specific hydraulic energy and in rotational speed are gradual and do not exceed the values stated in 5.2.1. If these requirements are satisfied, the mean value of the discharge calculated over the whole run shall be used; if they are not satisfied, the run shall be repeated, unless a suflicient period of time within the run duration may be found, during which the steadiness~of all the quantities involved is satisfied.

As far as possible, theindividual~readings of the discharge should be plotted against time to assess the nature and the extent of possible pulsations. 10.1.3.2 Leakage, inliltration or diversion As far as possible, leakage, infiltration or diversion of water shall be avoided between the measuring section or the measuring length and the relevant reference section. If this-cannot be avoided, the incoming or outgoing flow shall be measured with an appropriate accuracy. Whcncvcr a surge tank is connected to the waterway between the measuring section and the machine, water level oscillations should normally be allowed to damp out before a run is initiated. Should this be difficult due to the length of the waterway (and accordingly to the settling time), discharge measurcmcnt can however bc conducted, provided care is taken of the net volume of water exchanged between the duct and the surge tank within the duration of the measurement (for allowable variations of specific hydraulic energy, see 5.2). 10.2 Current-meter method 10.2.1 Principle of velocity-area method The velocity-area method requires a number of propeller-type current-meters located at specified points in a suitable cross-section of an open channel or closed conduit. Simultaneous measurements of local mean velocity with the meters are integrated over the gauging section to provide the discharge. The water must be suflicicntly clean, such that dissolved or suspended matter will not affect the accuracy of the meter readings during the test. Some integration tcchniqucs which may be used to compute the discharge assume velocity distributions that closely approximate known laws, especially in the ncighbourhood of solid boundaries. If thcsc techniques are used, it is csscntial to select a measuring section where this hypothesis is likely to bc approximately fultillcd. The method may bc used at any suitable measuring section in: a closed conduit or pcnstock, an intake slructurc; an upsucam or downstream open channel (headrace or tailrace).

If an open channel is to bc used, it must be an artificial channel of well-defined cross-section. Natural streams are cxcludcd for tests under this standard.

62

IS/IEC 41( l3991)

Test arrangements, procedures and limitations will depend to some extent on the characteristics of the sclcctcd measuring section. General rcquiremcnts applicable to all measuring sections arc given below.

10.2.2 General requirements 10.2.2.1 Duration of measurement Measurements for each current-mctcr position shall last at least 2 min. If variations (see 52.1) in the water velocity are present, a run shall include at least four cycles of these variations. This may have an influence on the entire test programme. The duration of variations may be determined by observing the speed changes of the current-meters for 10 to 15 min for at least two typical conditions of operation.

10.2.2.2 Number of measuring points The number of current-meters shall be sufficient to ensure a satisfactory determination of the velocity profile over the whole measuring section. A single-point measurement is not permitted under this standard. Set also IS0 3354.4.4.1 to 4.4.3. At least 13 measuring points shall be used in a circularpenstoek, one of which shall be the centre point of the section. The number of measuring points per radius, 2, excluding the centre point, may be determined from 4fi < 2 < 5fi where R is the internal radius of the conduit in metres. For any given number of current-meters, it is preferable to increase the number of radii than to increase tbe number of currentmeters per radius, but care must be taken to avoid excessive blockage. Centre blockage can bc reduced by cantilevering the radial supporting arms from the conduit wall. If this is done, only a single arm need extend to the centrc of the conduit. Little advantage is gained by measurements on more than 8 radii or at more than 8 points per radius, excluding the centre point. At lcast 25 measuring points shall be used in _a rectangular or trapezoidal section. If the velocity distribution is likely to be non-uniform, the number of measuring points, 2, shall be determined from:

whcrc: A is lhc arca of lhc measuring section in square metres

If the conduit or channel is divided into scvcral sections, measurcmcnts shallbc made simultaneously in all sections. 10.2.2.3 Types and gcncral rcquircmcnts of current-meters T)nly propcllcr-type current-mctcrs shall bc used. The electrical impulses of thcpropcllcr rotation shall bc transmitted by cables to the counting and recording device in such a way that lhc momentary speed of rotation of the propeller can bc checked during and after the run. The current-meters shall fuldl the applicable rcquiremcnts of IS0 2537. All meters shall be capable of withstanding the water pressure and the time of submcrgencc without change in the calibration. It may be necessary to rcducc the time of submcrgcncc whcrc the water is hard.

WIEC

41( 1991)

Cm-mm-meter propellers shall bc not less than 100 mm diameter cxccpt for measurements in the peripheral zone where propcllcrs as small as 50 mm may be used. The distance from the trailing edge of the propeller to the leading edge of the mounting rod shall be at least 150 mm. The angle bctwecn the local vclccity vector and the axis of the current-meter should not cxcccd 5". When larger angles are unavoidable, self-compensating propeilers which measure directly the axial component of the velocity shall be used but only at angles for which they have been designed and calibrated (see 6.1.5 in IS0 3354). The response of a current-meter can be affected by the axial and transverse components of the turbulence of the flow, and this effect cannot be taken into account during the calibration which is carried out in still water. Thus it is recommended to select the types of propeller which are the less sensitive to turbulcncc (propellers with a high moment of inertia). 10.2.2.4 Calibration of current-meters Subject to the requirements stated below, all current-meters shall bc calibrated in accordance with IS0 3455. The current-meters shall be calibrated with the same type of mounting and mounting rod as that used during the test. If the current-meters are mounted on vertical rods during calibration, these shall extend at least 150 mm below the propcllcr shaft. It is desirable to calibrate several current-meters at the same time mounted at the same distance as will bc used during the test. The range of calibration velocities shall, if possible, cover the range of local vclocitics during the test. A normal calibration range is from 0,4 m/s to 6 m/s or even 8 m/s, the upper limit often being set by vibration. If extrapolation of the rating curve beyond 20% of the maximum calibration velocity is ncccssary, it shall be done only by mutual agreement and with the understanding that uncertainty in the mcasuremcnt has been increased. Self-compensating propellers shall be calibrated at angles up to the maximum obliquity of the flow expected during the test and up to'the maximum expected test velocity, the relative direction of the mounting rod and the oblique flow being respected; no extrapolation is permitted. The estimated systematic uncertainty al 95% confidence level, due to current-meter calibration, should normally be less than 0,5% for velocities between 0,4 m/s and 6 m/s. Above and below those velocities, a greater uncertainty should be expected, depending on the characteristics of the calibration station and of the propellers. Notwithstanding the fact that 4.6.2 requests calibration before a test, this may be considered as fulfilled if the current-meters arc regularly calibrated showing consistent results. The time between calibrations depends on the duration and character of use of the current-meters. Three hundred hours of running time under favourablc water conditions may be taken as a guide. The Chief of test shall ascertain that no damage has occurred during the test, particularly deterioration caused by shocks, corrosion~or abrasion. A calibration of a current-meter is imperative after the test only if it would seem to have been damaged. 10.2.3 Measurements in closed conduifs (pensrocks) 10.2.3.1 Gcncral IS0 3354 shall apply subjcet to the restrictions given in 10.2.2 and 10.2.3.2.

10.2.4Measurements in short pensfocks or intake slructures 10.2.4.1 General

A pcnstock is defined as short if the straight length is less than 25 diameters. No existing standard deals with discharge measurements in short pcnstocks or intakes, especially for low-head plants. IS0 3354 may be used as a guide especially the clauses stating gcncral rcquircmenls and those dealing with rectangular cross-sections. Also applicable are the general requirements of 10.2.2 of the prcscnt standard. The main difficulty with this type of gauging arises from the fact that the~measuring section may be located in a short converging conduit with uneven and/or unstable velocity distributions as well as oblique flow to the current-meters. Attempts should be made to remedy lhcse difficulties either by a straightening device (set 10.2.4.2) or by special measuring techniques (see 10.2.4.3).

10.2.4.2 Bell-mouth nozzle A temporary bell-mouth nozzle (see Figure 24) may be installed at the entrance to the intake struclurc. The advantages arc: - a straight and parallel flow; a more nearly uniform and stable velocity distribution; an increase in both the mc`anvelocity and local velocities near the walls which incrcascs the accuracy at low loads; a bcttcr measuring section than can be had in an open approach channel since lhc Carca is constant and depth mcasurcmcnts arc climinatcd.

The disadvantages arc: the cost and difticulty of fabricating and installing such a structure; that the flow through the mod&d intake_may change the performance of the machine. The available lcsls indicate this to bc of littlc conscqucnce;

65

ISfIEC 41~(1991;) that the turbulent boundary layer thickness may be less than the distance from the wall to the outermost current-meter. This thickness shall bc determined by test or .calculation* and the discharge in the peripheral zone shall bc computed with due regard to the actual velocity distribution.

Figure 24 - Temporary nozzle or bell mouth placed in the intake of a low head turbine 10.2.4.3 Measurements in converging flow Measurements in converging conduits with velocities oblique to the cross-section shall be allowed only by mutual agreement of the parties to the test. Gauging methods have been devised to improve the accuracy but they require highly-experienced personnel and it is difficult to predict the systematic and random errors which may arise. In one method, the plane cross-section is replaced by an equipotential surface perpendicular to the streamlines. The surface may be determined by hydraulic or aerodynamic similitude or by electrical analogy. The current-meter axes are then aligned with the assumed velocity direction at each measuring point.

`The thickness, 6. of the turbulent boundary layer may be calculated by:

66

IS/IEC 41( 1991) Another method uses a plant cross-section together with an exploration of the angularity of the velocity field. During preliminary tests, at each measuring position, the current-meter is aligned successively in Iwo known directions and the velocities arc measured. Caution shall be taken to keep the propeller closely to the same location. This may imply moving the supporting frame. The actual direction of the velocity is calculated from these measurements and the angular response curve of the propcllcr. After that, each current-meter is aligned as closely as possible with the computed dircclion of the velocity at each position and the final measurement is made. Since individual adjustment of each current-mctcr may be difficult, some angularity may remain, that must be accounted for in the calculations. The angular exploration is conducted for two load conditions of the machine, or more if it appears that the velocity directions change with load. Self-compensating propellers (see 10.2.2.3) are best suited for this method, provided they fulfil other rcquircmcnts. Normal propcllcrs may be accepted if the flow is two-dimensional in the converging section.

10.2.4.4 Direct integration method This method is described in 7.2.2 and7.3.2 of IS0 3354, and shall be allowed only by mutual agrccmcnt of the parties to the test. In a rectangular conduit, a vertical or horizontal row of meters is moved across the cross-section at constant speed (see Figure 25). Any influcncc of the transverse vclocily on the measurements may be cstimatcd by rcvcrsing the direction of motion of the supporting frame and by mcasuremcnts with the frame at rest in several typical locations. Thcsc cheek runs should bc made at scvcral different flow rates. Special equipment is required for this method because the mctcrs must bc translated at constant speed and must also bc free of vibrations. Supplcmcntary stationary measurements near the invert or ceiling may be required if thcsc areas cannot be swept by the moving frame. Usually this method is advantageous only in conduits of very large crosssection.

10.2.5.4 Mounting of the current-meters All current-meters shall be rigidly attached to the mounting rods with the propeller axes exactly perpendicular to the plane of the measuring section. 10.3 Pitot tubes 10.3.1 General Pitot tubes may bc used to mcasurc the dynamic pressure, from which the local velocity may be obtained, at each of a sufficient number of points in the cross-section to permit computation of the discharge by the vclocily area method. Since the dynamic pressure varies with the square of the velocity, the accuracy of measurement decreases rapidly with decreasing velocity. In practical terms this restricts the use~of Pitot tubes to flow in closed conduits where the velocity is not too low and the water isfree of suspended matter.

10.3.2 Standardized Pitot tubes IS0 3966 covers the design, installation and use of standardized Pitot static tubes. Only the clauses relating to incompressible fluid shall be used for testing under this standard. Any signiticant blockage effect must be taken into account. The IS0 standard gives all the necessary guidance for the selection and installation of Pitot static tubes, choice of measuring section, and the computation of the discharge and its uncertainty. IS0 3966 shall be used only with the shdardized Pitct static tubes described therein which arc equipped with a single total pressure tap and one or more static pressure taps. 10.4 Pressure-time method 10.4.1 Principle of the method This method of discharge measurement (often called "Gibson method") is based upon Newton's law and the derived laws of fluid mechanics, which give the relation between the force due to the change of pressure difference between two sections and the acceleration or deceleration of the mass of water lxtwccn these sections due to a gate* movement. Although this method is theoretically valid both for turbine and pump operation and for closure or opening of the gate, it is in practice only used in case of discharge cut-off in turbine operation. The following is a simplified way of describing the pressure-time method principle. In a fluid without friction, a change of velocity dv/dt in a conduit of constant cross-section A. of a mass of fluid pLA would lead to a differential pressure Ap between the upstream (subscript u).and downstream (subscript d) cross-section of the considered length L:

10.4.2.4Checking of the pressure measurements

To ensure the necessary accuracy in the recorded pressure-time diagrams, flow conditions in the conduit shall be such that, at each measuring section, the difference between the pressure measured at any one tap and the average of the pressures measured at all taps shall not exceed 20% of the dynamic pressure. The average of the readings from any pair of oppositetaps shah not differ from the average from any other pair of taps in the same cross-section by more than 10 % of the dynamic pressure. This may require consideration of such items as velocity distribution, length of straight run of the conduit and wall conditions at the individual taps. If any pressure tap appears to be in error, the source of the discrepancy shall be dete.rmined and removed. If this is not possible, the tap shall not be used for the measurements. A minimum of two taps shall be used in each measuring section. These checks shall be carried out before the test begins. The special instrumentation required for that shall be immediately dismounted in order not to disturb the arrangement of the test apparatus and its connecting tubing (see 10.4.2.3). 10.4.3 Differential pressure-time method 10.4.3.1 Generalities In this variant, the change in differential pressure between two sections of measurement, that is affected only by the changes in friction and in momentum between these two sections, is recorded. The effects of changes in friction outside of-the test sections and in intake or surge tank water level are present at both measurement sections and are thus eliminated. In addition to the requirements specitied in 10.4.2.1, the product of the length between the two pressure measurement sections and the mean velocity in the pipe when the unit is carrying full load shall be not less than 50 m2/s. The discharge which is to be measured shall be fixed by means of the load limiting device or preferably ~by blocking the gates in the required position and waiting until stable conditions arc established (see 4.4.2 b)). The pressure-time function can then be obtained by gradually closing the gates in one continuous movement and recording the resultant time dependent change in differential pressure. The recording times before the beginning and after the end of the movement of the gate shall be not less lhan 20 s each. Before the test a calibration of the measuring system has to be done. At each run the zero point of the measuring system and the calibration when using transducers have to be chcckcd. 10.4.3.2 DiffcrentirLmercury pressure-gauge (Gibson apparatus) 10.4.3.2.1 Principle of me apparatus

This was the first measuring system used for the pressure-time method. This apparatus delivers a pressure-time diagram in the form of a photographic record of the mercury level movement in a U-tube manometer. The integral J Ap adt is thus obtained by planimetry.

In this variant of the pressure-time method, the changes in pressure at two measurcmcnt cross-sections of the penstock are recorded separately. It is also possible to use only one measurement section referred to the intake free surface, but such a method can only be used where a surge chamber is not provided and where the length of the penstock, for which the calculationof the pipe factor is difficult(intakeb&mouth, etc.) does not exceed-2 96 of the whole length. In addition to the requirements specified in 10.4.2.1, the length of penstock between the two pressure measuring sections shall be not less than 50 m and the pipe factor F of the penstock from the surgechamber to the lower measuring section shall be not less than four times that from the surge chamber to the upper measuring section. The mode of operation is practically the same as previously described in 10.4.3. The equipment used in this cast is shown schematically in Figure 30 and comprises: a water pressure measuring device at each measurement section; a calibration dcvicc for the pressure measuring device; a lime measuring dcvicc; measuring devices of the water level and of its variation in the surge chamber; arccording device.

All parts of the pressure measuring and recording devices shall conform to the requirements stated in 10.4.3.3.1. The following must bcrecordcd on each run: the calibration diagrams of the measuring pressure device before and after the gate closure; the prcssurc-time diagrams before, during and after this closure (at least four pressure waves shall be recorded after the completion of the closure); the surge chamber water level-time diagram or the steady-state level after closure, when only one measuring section is used. 10.5 Tracer methods 10.5.1 General Three basic methods exist: two, the "constant-rate-injection method" and the "intcgralion (sudden injcction)~method", use the dilution principle and the third, known as the "transit-time method", is based on a measurement of the time taken for a tracer to travel a specified distance bctwecn two cross-sections in a pipe or in an open-channel. However, in the present state of knowledge, and for the purpose of this standard, only the constant-rate-injection method and transit-time method, in closed conduit, arc recommended. Moreover, the transit-time method is to be preferred to the constant-rate-injection method, due to the spurious and random errors which can arise when using the latter.

Standards are available for these methods using both radioactive and non-radioactive tracers. Refcrencc is made where appropriate in the sub-clauses below to those standards which can bc used, within the limits given, for acceptance~tests on hydraulic turbines and storage pumps. The methods are particularly suitable where there are relatively long lengths of penstock available or where additional mixing of the tracer may be obtained by inclusion of the machine in the measuring length or the installation of mixing-promoters (cg. turbulators), as the machine alone does not provide sufficient mixing.

.10.5.2 Constant-rate-injection method 10.5.2.1 Principle of the method The principle of lhis method of discharge~mcasurement is the continuous injection of a tracer into lhc main water flow at a steady mcasurcd rate and the determination of the resulting concentration of tmccr, rclalivc to its initial concentration, at a point far enough downstream to ensure thorough mixing. It is not ncccssary to know the gcomctric characteristics of the pipe but it is essential to cnsurc that rcvcrse or side currents do not exist which could abort some of the tracer. Also, conccntradon of the tracer in natural waler must bc constant and not exceed 15 % of the concentration at the sampling point during injection of the tracer. The discharge~Q can be dctcrmined from:

Q=qc, where: Q is 4 is Co is C, is C, is the the the the the discharge to bc mcasurcd discharge of tracer solution injected initial concentration of tracer in natural water concentration of tracer in the injected fluid concentration of tracer at the sampling station

10.5.2.2 Application of the method Radioactive and non-radioactive tracers can be used, provided the rccommcndations and proccdurcs described in Parts 1,2~and 3 of IS0 2975 arc applied.

10.5.2.3Uncertainty of mcasuremcnt (see 10.1.2)

The IS0 standard rcfcrred to in 10.5.2.2 gives all the necessary requirements for a successful mcasurcment but does not give a speciIic limit on the uncertainty of the resulting measurcmcnt. It is rcquircd to estimate the individual sources of systematic errors in each of the component measurements and combine these wilh Iherandom errors by the method given to obtain an estimate of the total unccrtaimy. When applying these methods to the measurement of the discharge through hydraulic machines during acceptance tests, it is important that the strictest limitations given in the relevant standard are observed. Suitable tests must be carried out to check that the tracer and measurement equipment arc suitable for Ihc particular conditions of the installation and the flow distribution in the measuring length is acceptable. With good measuring techniques and flow conditions, the estimated systematic uncertainly at 95 % confidence level should be about fl % to f2 I. 10.5.3 Transit-lime method 10.5.3.1 Principle of this method The transit-time method (formerly called lhe "Allen salt velocity method") is based on lhc mcasurcmcnt of the transit time of "labellcd" fluid particles between two cross-sections of Lhcconduit a known distance apart.
